newsitem.title: USA: Quit-smoking products could thrive after settlement.
newsitem.headline: Quit-smoking products could thrive after settlement.

text.p: The $750 million market for drugs and devices to help people stop smoking could easily double within two years if a key proposal in the tobacco settlement talks is accepted, industry analysts said.

Health groups, state attorneys general and lawyers for smokers suing tobacco companies have suggested that any settlement require the tobacco industry to finance programs for smokers who want to quit.

Under one proposal from a group of law firms handling class-action suits on behalf of addicted smokers, a tobacco industry fund would be tapped to pay up to $600 apiece for individuals seeking treatment, according to published reports.

"Sales in the U.S. for all types of this kind of therapy could double within two years if smokers are given free access to treatment," said James Keeney, a drug industry analyst for the Boston firm of Rodman & Renshaw.
"Most of the world's market for this type of treatment is in the United States because other countries don't give them the priority we have here," Keeney said.

He said British drug company SmithKline Beecham Plc was likely to continue holding the lion's share of the U.S. market with its Nicorette chewing gum and Nicoderm skin patch -- both of which deliver nicotine in preset doses to help curb craving for the drug.

"We have 90 percent of the market," said SmithKline Beecham spokesman Richard Koenig, who noted both products had been prescription drugs until 1996 when they won Food and Drug Administration approval to be sold over the counter.

He refused to speculate how sales might be affected by adoption of the tobacco settlement proposal. But he said Nicorette and Nicoderm have each recently had sales of $6 million a week, most of that in the United States.

Edmund Debler, a drug analyst at Mehta and Isaly of New York, also said the settlement proposal would double the U.S. market for smoking cessation products within two years. But he said prescribed drugs would capture the biggest windfalls.

"The likely boon would be in prescription drugs because people will take the higher-tech route if someone else pays and because it would be a surer way of documenting their treatment for reimbursement."

Johnson & Johnson's McNeil Consumer Products Co. has brought three smoking-cessation therapies to the market since 1996, including its over-the-counter Nicotrol patch. McNeil also sells two prescription drugs, Nicotrol nasal spray and the Nicotrol Inhaler -- a nicotine inhalation system.
A McNeil spokesman declined to comment on the tobacco-settlement proposal and said sales figures were not immediately available.
Debler said Glaxo Wellcome Plc also stood to gain from the settlement proposal, through sales of Zyban tablets manufactured by its U.S. subsidiary.
Glaxo in May won FDA permission for U.S. sales of the drug, also marketed for depression under the name Wellbutrin, as the first nicotine-free prescription medicine for smoking cessation.
Debler said Zyban, which he had estimated would post $40 million in sales in 1997, would do far better if the settlement proposal is put into action.

Negotiators are entering what they believe will be a make-or-break week to settle the huge claims against the tobacco industry as they try to reach a deal before the first state Medicaid case goes to trial in Mississippi next month.
